header.deal: Ticket seller running arena tour on-sales
header.incumbent: Unnamed payments provider whose support was a ticket form
header.tag_why: Halima was comparing who picks up when a payment fails on an on-sale. The competitor put named people in the room and promised on-call cover, while our tiers and response times read to her as 'a queue with a faster timer'.

messaging_changes.current_line: Support plans with tiered response times, up to 24/7 coverage.
messaging_changes.change: For operations buyers at event-driven merchants, lead with 'A name, not a queue.' Introduce the named people on the account (solutions engineer and account lead), have them in the room, and put their names in the proposal. Then say who covers their biggest days. Only promise on-call cover for peak events if we can actually staff it. Do not open with tiers or response times when the buyer asks who.
messaging_changes.why: When Halima asked 'who's my person' she was walked through the support plans, which is essentially M5. She dismissed it as 'a queue with a faster timer'. The competitor won by putting named people in the room.

messaging_changes.change: Add a peak-event proof asset for event-driven merchants: a written plan for their on-sale morning, built with the solutions engineer before the decision meeting. It should state who is watching, who they call, and what happens at minute four. Suggested line: 'I don't buy uptime, I buy what happens when it's down.' Here is exactly what happens on your on-sale morning.
messaging_changes.why: The decider explicitly asked to see on paper what we do on an on-sale morning. The rep said we have no such asset and that he could have built one with our SE.

messaging_changes.current_line: Trusted by leading businesses; see our customer stories.
messaging_changes.change: For operations buyers, replace logo-led proof with a reference customer who can name the person who picked up when something went wrong on their biggest day. Offer it as a call, not a case study.
messaging_changes.why: The rep says 'I had logos. I didn't have a person.' The customer's pain was a provider whose support never picked up, so logos did not answer the decider's question.

messaging_changes.change: For event-driven merchants, open on incident ownership ahead of M1's global-growth line. Ask what happened the last time payments failed during a live sale, and who answered. Treat sandbox and load-test proof as the price of entry for the operations buyer, and keep it in the technical track with the CTO.
messaging_changes.why: The evaluation was triggered by an unanswered ticket form during a public on-sale failure, not by throughput. The decider met the load-test results with a single 'good.'

trigger.insight: Payments had already failed during on-sales twice, according to Ben, and the customer did not switch. The evaluation began only when the failure became public, reached the CEO, and nobody at the provider picked up until it was over. The pain that drove the buy was the unanswered ticket form, not throughput. We pitched to the minute-four failure, but the COO was buying against the reply that came after the on-sale ended.
trigger.messaging: For event-driven merchants, open on what happens in the first minutes of an incident on their biggest day, ahead of M1's global growth line.

decider.insight: Halima started the replacement and Halima ended it, yet our proof was built for Ben, who ran the load test. Our status as 'the favourite' existed only in the champion's eyes, and the decider overruled him in a single meeting. We had access to Halima. What we lacked was a story aimed at her criteria.
decider.messaging: Give the COO her own narrative about incident ownership and escalation, separate from the CTO's technical proof.

competitor.insight: The competitor won the evaluation by changing its questions, not by matching our platform. After their meeting, the customer's criteria moved from throughput, queueing and bots to names, a ground where our tier sheet had nothing to offer. The rep's view that they over-promised is unverified, and it misses the point: a staffing promise answered Halima's question, and we gave her no answer at all.
competitor.messaging: Bring the actual account team into the room and name them in the proposal, rather than arguing that a competitor's on-call promise can't be kept.

message.insight: Everything that landed (sandbox, docs, uptime, bot and fraud tooling) landed with the engineers. The one message the decider heard, tiered response times, is almost word for word our M5, and she took it apart in one sentence. M5 talks about how quickly a ticket gets answered. She wanted to know whose phone rings.
message.messaging: Rewrite M5 from 'tiered response times' into a named team plus explicit peak-event coverage, and stop opening with tiers when the buyer asks 'who'.

decided.insight: The rep believed the load test had won the deal. Halima's one-word 'good' was the warning sign: to her, technical proof was table stakes, not the deciding factor. The deal turned the moment our answer to 'who's my person' turned out to be a process, not a person.
decided.messaging: Treat platform and load-test proof as the price of entry with operations buyers, and spend the decision meeting on the incident-response story.

gaps.insight: Neither gap was a product gap. The first was a missing document: a written on-sale plan the rep says he could have built with our SE. The second was a missing reference: someone who could say who picked up, where we only had logos. Both gaps are about proving a human response, and our M8 'customer stories' proof is built on logos, which is exactly what failed here.
gaps.messaging: Build a peak-event runbook template (who's watching, who you call, what happens at minute four) and a reference customer who can name the person who picked up.

language.insight: Our vocabulary (support plans, tiers, response times, uptime) is exactly what the customer was rejecting. Their unit of value is a person on 'on-sale morning', and Halima explicitly ruled out uptime as a buying criterion. Even the word 'support' put us in the queue category she dismissed.
language.messaging: Replace 'support plans' and 'uptime' with 'a name, not a queue' and 'what happens when it's down' framing for event-critical merchants.

gaps.follow_up: Ask Jordan, or Ben if needed, which vendor Halima chose.

gaps.question: Does the competitor actually staff someone on call for every major on-sale?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Ben after the spring on-sales whether the competitor's on-call person and shared channel showed up.

gaps.question: Did Halima ever meet a named person from our side (SE, account lead) before deciding?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Jordan who from our team was in the room with Halima, and whether anyone was named as her contact.

gaps.question: Was there any chance to come back with an on-sale plan after the 'queue with a faster timer' remark?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Jordan how much time passed between that meeting and the decision, and whether Ben could have taken a revised plan to Halima.

close.rep_takeaway: Ben's criteria weren't Halima's. When the decider asks 'who's my person', answer with a name and a written plan, not a tier sheet. If you notice an asset is missing that you could build with your SE, build it before the decision meeting, not after the loss.
